To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

CD44-specific antibodies trigger rapid depletion of granulocytes from the circulation in a CD44 cross-link-dependent manner and that this depletion is associated with a rapid abrogation of leukocyte rolling in the inflamed joints.

CD44-specific antibody treatment, which has been considered a promising therapeutic strategy, exerts disparate effects on leukocyt recruitment in experimental arthritis, and that these effects are mediated through engagement of the granulocyte coagulation system and subsequent depletion of these cells in circulation.

CD44 deficiency increases leukocyte rolling in inflamed joints, whereas CD44-specific antibodies trigger granulocyte elimination in the circulation, and that both effects can be reproduced with an anti-Gr-1 antibody.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the pathogenesis of rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis, two autoimmune diseases that are associated with chronic inflammation in joints and the skin
the molecular basis and therapeutic potential of CD44-specific anti-inflammatory antibodies.
the role of the cell adhesion molecule CD44 and other molecules in the pathogenesis of rheumatoid diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the anti-inflammatory effect of anti-CD44 antibodies is primarily the result on the depletion of granulocytes.

CD44 deficiency does indeed have an anti-inflammatory effect on arthritis, but this is not a result of the absence of CD44 on leukocytes, but rather the result of the presence of CD44 on endothelial cells.
anti-CD44 mAbs are effective in arthritis, but not through their ability to inhibit leukocyte recruitment, as previously assumed, but rather by triggering the depletion of granulocytes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anti-CD44 antibodies are effective in the treatment of inflammatory arthritis, but the mechanism of action is different from what was initially believed.
CD44 deficiency does protect against inflammation, but that CD44-specific antibody treatment is a more potent anti-arthritic strategy.
the anti-inflammatory effect of anti-CD44 treatment is not mediated via inhibition of CD44-CD44 interactions, but rather via CD44 cross-link-induced granulocyte depletion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CD44-specific antibodies exert a rapid and profound effect on the trafficking and survival of granulocytes in inflamed joints, which is not observed with CD44 deficiency.

CD44-specific antibodies, which have been considered a promising therapeutic approach for inflammatory diseases, may exert their effect through a previously uncharacterized mechanism, namely, the induction of granulocyte depletion in the circulation.
CD44-specific antibody therapy may not be effective against other immune-mediated disorders that are associated with a different pattern of leukocyte recruitment in the inflamed tissue.
